clinician.trajectory_summary: A male teenager presented with a 7-year history of slowly progressive asymptomatic swelling over the nape of the neck, with intermittent discharge and difficulty in neck mobility and mouth opening. A cutaneous punch biopsy revealed colonies of filamentous bacteria with a Splendore–Hoeppli reaction and suppurative granulation tissue, and Gram’s stain showed filamentous gram-positive bacilli. Aerobic, anaerobic, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures were negative, strongly supporting a diagnosis of actinomycosis. Initial treatment with injection ceftriaxone and oral penicillin G led to a temporary 20% improvement, but the swelling recurred and worsened. A repeat CE-MRI showed disease progression with increased pachymeningeal thickening and involvement of various head and neck spaces. A revised diagnosis of actinomycetoma was made, and the patient was started on intravenous amikacin, oral rifampicin, and cotrimoxazole. A subsequent MRI after 20 days of this therapy showed mixed results, with some areas improving and others worsening. The patient was then switched to intravenous linezolid, ceftriaxone, and steroids (dexamethasone, then oral prednisolone), which resulted in a drastic decrease in swelling within 7 days. At discharge, the patient was prescribed a regimen of oral prednisolone, penicillin G, doxycycline, and metronidazole. One month post-discharge, the swelling had decreased by 60%.
